passage:
"You've been weird all week," Omkar said, stirring his tea. "Did I do something?"
"No. It's me." Hemant looked at the cups. "I need to tell you something and I'm scared it'll wreck things."
"Try me."
"Somewhere in the last year you stopped being just my friend for me. I like you, like that. You don't have to say anything now. Whatever you say, I still want us to be friends. I was tired of hiding it and getting annoyed at you for not knowing."
Omkar was quiet. "Wow. Okay. Thank you for not making me guess."
"Take your time."
"I honestly need a few days to think. Is that alright?"
"Yes. And if the answer is no, I'll be okay. Sad, but okay."
Omkar bumped Hemant's shoulder. "Same time Sunday, same stall?"

qa.q: What was Omkar doing when he asked Hemant if he had done something?
Why was Hemant scared to speak?
qa.a: He feared telling Omkar would wreck the friendship. He had also been hiding his feelings and getting annoyed at Omkar for not knowing.

qa.q: What did Hemant do that lets Omkar answer freely, and what could he do while waiting?
qa.a: He said he wanted to stay friends whatever the answer and told Omkar to take his time. While waiting he can give space and not push.

qa.q: How might Omkar be feeling when he asks for a few days?
qa.a: Omkar seems surprised and thoughtful, perhaps unsure of his own feelings. He thanked Hemant for not making him guess and suggested Sunday at the stall, so he values the friendship.

grounding: A close friend has become more than a friend; the protagonist tells them without pressure and accepts either answer.
